item.title: Go Daily Question 108
item.description:
Regarding type conversion, which of the following options is correct?

A.
type MyInt int
var i int = 1
var j MyInt = i

B.
type MyInt int
var i int = 1
var j MyInt = (MyInt)i

C.
type MyInt int
var i int = 1
var j MyInt = MyInt(i)

D.
type MyInt int
var i int = 1
var j MyInt = i.(MyInt)
🔑 Answer Analysis:

C

item.title: Go Daily Question 089
item.description:
What is the output of the following code? Why?

func (i int) PrintInt ()  {
    fmt.Println(i)
}

func main() {
    var i int = 1
    i.PrintInt()
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

It will result in a compilation error. Methods can only be created for custom types and must be defined within the same package as the type.

Reference Answer and Analysis: B.

Methods based on a type must be defined within the same package. The code above creates a PrintInt() method based on the int type. Since int type and the PrintInt() method are defined in different packages, it results in a compilation error. A solution is to define a new type:

item.title: Go Daily Question 024
item.description:
Will the following code compile? If so, what will be the output?

package main

import "fmt"

type MyInt1 int
type MyInt2 = int

func main() {
    var i int =0
    var i1 MyInt1 = i 
    var i2 MyInt2 = i
    fmt.Println(i1,i2)
}
🔑 Answer Analysis:

Answer: No. Reference analysis: This question tests the difference between type aliases and type definitions. Type alias: type MyInt2 = int Type definition: type MyInt1 int In Go, the types on both sides of the assignment operator = must be consistent. MyInt1 is a new type defined based on int, so it cannot be directly assigned. If an assignment is needed, type conversion is required: var i1 MyInt1 = MyInt1(i)
